The Legendre potential and the gradient case of the differential Galois criterion for the Jacobian conjecture

Elżbieta Adamus Address: Faculty of Applied Mathematics, AGH University of Krakow, al. Mickiewicza 30, 30-059 Kraków, Poland Email address: esowa@agh.edu.pl and Zbigniew Hajto Address: Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, ul. Łojasiewicza 6, 30-348 Kraków, Poland Email address: zbigniew.hajto@uj.edu.pl
Abstract.

Let h∈ℂ⁡[X1,…,Xn]h\in\mathbb{C}[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}] have constant nonzero Hessian determinant, let h∗h^{*} be its formal Legendre transform and g=⟨X,∇h⟩−hg=\langle X,\nabla h\rangle-h. The Nambu derivations of ∇h\nabla h satisfy δi​(g)=Xi\delta_{i}(g)=X_{i} and δα​(g)=(∂αh∗)∘∇h\delta^{\alpha}(g)=(\partial^{\alpha}h^{*})\circ\nabla h. Consequently, in the gradient case the differential Galois criterion of [5], consisting of nn membership conditions, reduces to a single membership condition. Equivalently, ∇h\nabla h is a polynomial automorphism if and only if g∈ℂ⁡[∂1h,…,∂nh]g\in\mathbb{C}[\partial_{1}h,\dots,\partial_{n}h]. Moreover, ∇h\nabla h is a polynomial automorphism if and only if δα​(g)=0\delta^{\alpha}(g)=0 for |α|=(deg⁡h−1)n−1+2|\alpha|=(\deg h-1)^{n-1}+2, and then the coefficients δα​(g)​(x0)/α!\delta^{\alpha}(g)(x_{0})/\alpha! of h∗h^{*} at ∇h​(x0)\nabla h(x_{0}) determine the inverse. If the Hessian determinant of hh is merely a nonzero polynomial, then gg is still a primitive element of ℂ⁡(X)\mathbb{C}(X) over ℂ⁡(∂1h,…,∂nh)\mathbb{C}(\partial_{1}h,\dots,\partial_{n}h). For the Nambu-tower criterion, doubling a Keller map yields no independent conditions. After an affine change of coordinates putting ∇h\nabla h in the normal form X+HX+H, the formal Legendre transform is the sum of the formal Pascal difference series of gg, and the termination of this series implies polynomial invertibility. In at most three variables the normal form of every gradient Keller map has strongly nilpotent Jacobian part and is therefore Pascal finite, by a theorem of de Bondt, and an explicit gradient automorphism in four variables has a normal form which is not Pascal finite. The five-variable counterexample of Meng and Yang shows that the properties used here do not imply the Hessian conjecture. The results do not settle the open cases JC2\mathrm{JC}_{2} and HC4\mathrm{HC}_{4}.

Key words and phrases: 
Jacobian conjecture, Hessian conjecture, Nambu derivations, Legendre transform, Picard–Vessiot theory, Pascal finite automorphisms, cotangent lift
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14R15; Secondary 12H05, 13N15, 37J30

1. Introduction

Throughout, 𝕜\Bbbk is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and 𝕜⁡[X]=𝕜⁡[X1,…,Xn]\Bbbk[X]=\Bbbk[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]. A polynomial map F:𝕜n→𝕜nF\colon\Bbbk^{n}\to\Bbbk^{n} is a Keller map if detJ​F∈𝕜×\det JF\in\Bbbk^{\times}. The Jacobian conjecture JCn\mathrm{JC}_{n} asserts that every Keller map 𝕜n→𝕜n\Bbbk^{n}\to\Bbbk^{n} has a polynomial inverse [18, 9, 29]. A polynomial h∈𝕜⁡[X]h\in\Bbbk[X] with detHess⁡h∈𝕜×\det\operatorname{Hess}h\in\Bbbk^{\times} is called a Keller potential, and the Hessian conjecture HCn\mathrm{HC}_{n} of Meng [20] asserts that the formal Legendre transform of every Keller potential in nn variables is a polynomial. The implications JCn⇒HCn\mathrm{JC}_{n}\Rightarrow\mathrm{HC}_{n} and HC2​n⇒JCn\mathrm{HC}_{2n}\Rightarrow\mathrm{JC}_{n} are elementary [20, 21].11 1 In July 2026 L. Alpöge announced an explicit Keller map 𝕜3→𝕜3\Bbbk^{3}\to\Bbbk^{3} which is not injective; see [21, Section 1]. Hence JCn\mathrm{JC}_{n} fails for n≥3n\geq 3. Meng and Yang [21] deduced that HCn\mathrm{HC}_{n} fails for n≥5n\geq 5, HC2\mathrm{HC}_{2} holds by [16] and HC3\mathrm{HC}_{3} by [13]. The cases JC2\mathrm{JC}_{2} and HC4\mathrm{HC}_{4} remain open, and HC4⇒JC2\mathrm{HC}_{4}\Rightarrow\mathrm{JC}_{2}. For potentials of degree at most four in four variables HC4\mathrm{HC}_{4} is proved in [24], and in Lorentzian signature for degree at most five in [19].

The present paper continues two lines of work. In the first, Crespo and the second author [15] introduced the Nambu derivations δ1,…,δn\delta_{1},\dots,\delta_{n} of a Keller map FF, characterized by δi​(Fj)=δi​j\delta_{i}(F_{j})=\delta_{ij}, and proved that FF is invertible if and only if 𝕜⁡(X)\Bbbk(X) with these derivations is a Picard–Vessiot extension of 𝕜\Bbbk. In [3] this was turned into an effective criterion through generalized Wronskians, tested by the algebra membership algorithm of [26], and in [5] into the surjectivity of a map φ:K⊗𝕜E→K⊗𝕜R\varphi\colon K\otimes_{\Bbbk}E\to K\otimes_{\Bbbk}R, which reduces to the nn conditions 1⊗Xi∈im⁡φ1\otimes X_{i}\in\operatorname{im}\varphi. In the second line [1, 2, 4, 7] the inverse is computed by the Pascal difference operator ΔF​(P)=P∘F−P\Delta_{F}(P)=P\circ F-P. Automorphisms FF with ΔFm​(X)=0\Delta_{F}^{m}(X)=0 for some mm are called Pascal finite [2]. They include the maps X+HX+H with strongly nilpotent J​HJH [7, Theorem 5.1], and the alternating Pascal series computes the formal inverse of any F=X+HF=X+H [6]. The cotangent lift of vector fields, which reappears below in the doubling construction, was used by the second author and Mohseni in a differential Galois study of non-integrable gradient systems [17]. The present paper studies both constructions when F=∇hF=\nabla h is a gradient.

Theorem (single condition, Theorem 4.3).

Let hh be a Keller potential and g=⟨X,∇h⟩−hg=\langle X,\nabla h\rangle-h. Then δi​(g)=Xi\delta_{i}(g)=X_{i} for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, and ∇h\nabla h is a polynomial automorphism if and only if 1⊗g∈im⁡φ1\otimes g\in\operatorname{im}\varphi, where φ\varphi is the map of [5] recalled in Section 3.

Theorem (Nambu tower of the Legendre potential, Theorem 4.7).

Let hh be a Keller potential of degree d≥2d\geq 2 and N=(d−1)n−1+2N=(d-1)^{n-1}+2. For every multi-index α\alpha one has δα​(g)=(∂αh∗)∘∇h\delta^{\alpha}(g)=(\partial^{\alpha}h^{*})\circ\nabla h. Consequently, ∇h\nabla h is a polynomial automorphism if and only if δα​(g)=0\delta^{\alpha}(g)=0 for all |α|=N|\alpha|=N, and in that case

h∗​(p)=∑|α|<Nδα​(g)​(x0)α!​(p−∇h​(x0))α,(∇h)−1=∇h∗,h^{*}(p)=\sum_{|\alpha|<N}\frac{\delta^{\alpha}(g)(x_{0})}{\alpha!}\,\bigl(p-\nabla h(x_{0})\bigr)^{\alpha},\qquad(\nabla h)^{-1}=\nabla h^{*},

for any point x0∈𝕜nx_{0}\in\Bbbk^{n}.

Theorem (Legendre potential of the doubling, Theorem 5.4).

Let F=X+HF=X+H be a Keller map and ΦF​(x,y)=⟨y,F⁡(x)⟩\Phi_{F}(x,y)=\langle y,F(x)\rangle. Then ⟨(x,y),∇ΦF⟩−ΦF=⟨y,x⟩+⟨y,ℰ⁡(H)⟩\langle(x,y),\nabla\Phi_{F}\rangle-\Phi_{F}=\langle y,x\rangle+\langle y,\mathcal{E}(H)\rangle, where ℰ=∑jXj∂j\mathcal{E}=\sum_{j}X_{j}\partial_{j}. In particular, if HH is homogeneous of degree mm, the Legendre potential of ΦF\Phi_{F} equals ⟨y,x⟩+m​fH\langle y,x\rangle+m\,f_{H}, where fH​(x,y)=⟨y,H⁡(x)⟩f_{H}(x,y)=\langle y,H(x)\rangle is the momentum function of HH whose Hamiltonian vector field is the cotangent lift of HH.

By the same identity δi​(g)=Xi\delta_{i}(g)=X_{i}, the polynomial gg is a primitive element of the field extension 𝕜⁡(X)⊃𝕜⁡(∂1h,…,∂nh)\Bbbk(X)\supset\Bbbk(\partial_{1}h,\dots,\partial_{n}h) for every hh with nonzero Hessian determinant (Theorem 4.15). For a Keller potential, ∇h\nabla h is therefore a polynomial automorphism if and only if gg lies in the subalgebra, or even in the subfield, generated by ∂1h,…,∂nh\partial_{1}h,\dots,\partial_{n}h (Theorem 4.17). The membership test of Shannon and Sweedler then returns h∗h^{*} itself.

The last theorem has a sharper form (Proposition 5.2 and Corollary 5.5). The Legendre transform of ΦF\Phi_{F} is ⟨u,F−1​(v)⟩\langle u,F^{-1}(v)\rangle, and the Nambu tower of ∇ΦF\nabla\Phi_{F} applied to its Legendre potential reduces to the Nambu tower of FF applied to the coordinates. The doubling therefore carries no information beyond the criterion for FF itself. In Section 6 we apply the inversion series of [6] to the identity h∗∘∇h=gh^{*}\circ\nabla h=g and write the Legendre transform as the sum of the Pascal series ∑k(−1)k​Δk​(g)\sum_{k}(-1)^{k}\Delta^{k}(g). Using a theorem of de Bondt [13], we show that in at most three variables the normal form of a gradient Keller map is X+HX+H with J​HJH strongly nilpotent, hence Pascal finite (Theorem 6.8). We give a Keller potential ϕ0\phi_{0} in four variables whose gradient is an automorphism with a normal form which is not Pascal finite, and whose inverse is returned by the membership test. Section 7 shows by the five-variable potential of [21] that the properties of Keller potentials used in this paper do not imply HCn\mathrm{HC}_{n} for n≥5n\geq 5. The reduction to gg does not lower the order NN of the tower (Remark 4.8). None of the results settles JC2\mathrm{JC}_{2} or HC4\mathrm{HC}_{4}.

2. Nambu derivations

Let FF be a Keller map, R=𝕜⁡[X]R=\Bbbk[X] and K=𝕜⁡(X)K=\Bbbk(X). The Nambu derivations of FF are defined by

(1) (δ1,…,δn)𝖳=((JF)−1)𝖳(∂1,…,∂n)𝖳,that isδi=∑k=1n((JF)−1)k​i∂k,(\delta_{1},\dots,\delta_{n})^{\mathsf{T}}=((JF)^{-1})^{\mathsf{T}}(\partial_{1},\dots,\partial_{n})^{\mathsf{T}},\qquad\text{that is}\qquad\delta_{i}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}((JF)^{-1})_{ki}\,\partial_{k},

see [15, 5]. Since (J​F)−1=(detJ​F)−1​adj⁡J​F(JF)^{-1}=(\det JF)^{-1}\operatorname{adj}JF has polynomial entries, δi​(R)⊂R\delta_{i}(R)\subset R.

Lemma 2.1.
  1. (i)

    δi​(Fj)=δi​j\delta_{i}(F_{j})=\delta_{ij} for all i,ji,j.

  2. (ii)

    For every formal power series P∈𝕜⁡[[p−p0]]P\in\Bbbk[[p-p_{0}]] and every x0x_{0} with F⁡(x0)=p0F(x_{0})=p_{0} one has δi​(P∘F)=(∂iP)∘F\delta_{i}(P\circ F)=(\partial_{i}P)\circ F in 𝕜⁡[[X−x0]]\Bbbk[[X-x_{0}]].

  3. (iii)

    The derivations δ1,…,δn\delta_{1},\dots,\delta_{n} commute pairwise.

  4. (iv)

    Each δi\delta_{i} has zero divergence, ∑k∂k(((J​F)−1)k​i)=0\sum_{k}\partial_{k}\bigl(((JF)^{-1})_{ki}\bigr)=0.

Proof.

(ii) By the chain rule ∂k(P∘F)=∑j(∂jP∘F)​(J​F)j​k\partial_{k}(P\circ F)=\sum_{j}(\partial_{j}P\circ F)(JF)_{jk}, hence δi​(P∘F)=∑j(∂jP∘F)​∑k(J​F)j​k​((J​F)−1)k​i=(∂iP)∘F\delta_{i}(P\circ F)=\sum_{j}(\partial_{j}P\circ F)\sum_{k}(JF)_{jk}((JF)^{-1})_{ki}=(\partial_{i}P)\circ F. Item (i) is the case P=pjP=p_{j}. (iii) The substitution P↦P∘FP\mapsto P\circ F is an isomorphism 𝕜⁡[[p−p0]]→𝕜⁡[[X−x0]]\Bbbk[[p-p_{0}]]\to\Bbbk[[X-x_{0}]], since the linear part of FF at x0x_{0} is invertible. By (ii) it transports ∂i\partial_{i} to δi\delta_{i} on 𝕜⁡[[X−x0]]\Bbbk[[X-x_{0}]], and the ∂i\partial_{i} commute. As R⊂𝕜⁡[[X−x0]]R\subset\Bbbk[[X-x_{0}]], the restrictions to RR commute, hence so do the extensions to KK. (iv) (J​F)−1=c−1​adj⁡(J​F)(JF)^{-1}=c^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(JF) with c=detJ​Fc=\det JF, so it suffices to prove the Piola identity ∑k∂kadj⁡(J​F)k​i=0\sum_{k}\partial_{k}\operatorname{adj}(JF)_{ki}=0 for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. Let Mi​kM_{ik} be the minor of J​FJF obtained by deleting row ii and column kk, so that adj⁡(J​F)k​i=(−1)i+k​Mi​k\operatorname{adj}(JF)_{ki}=(-1)^{i+k}M_{ik}. Consider the closed (n−1)(n-1)-form

ωi=d​F1∧⋯∧d​Fi^∧⋯∧d​Fn=∑kMi​k​d​X1∧⋯∧d​Xk^∧⋯∧d​Xn.\omega_{i}=dF_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge\widehat{dF_{i}}\wedge\dots\wedge dF_{n}=\sum_{k}M_{ik}\,dX_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge\widehat{dX_{k}}\wedge\dots\wedge dX_{n}.

Then

0=d​ωi=∑k(−1)k−1​∂kMi​k​d​X1∧⋯∧d​Xn=(−1)i+1​∑k∂kadj⁡(J​F)k​i​d​X1∧⋯∧d​Xn.0=d\omega_{i}=\sum_{k}(-1)^{k-1}\partial_{k}M_{ik}\,dX_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge dX_{n}=(-1)^{i+1}\sum_{k}\partial_{k}\operatorname{adj}(JF)_{ki}\,dX_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge dX_{n}.

∎

Remark 2.2.

The commutativity of the δi\delta_{i}, which is implicit in the Picard–Vessiot setting of [15, 5], is proved in (iii) without a separability argument. Statement (i) and the definition (1) make sense over any field in which detJ​F\det JF is a unit. By (iv), over ℝ\mathbb{R} the operators −−1​δi-\sqrt{-1}\,\delta_{i} are formally symmetric on compactly supported smooth functions, and by (i) and (iii) the assignment Xi↦FiX_{i}\mapsto F_{i}, ∂j↦δj\partial_{j}\mapsto\delta_{j} defines an endomorphism of the Weyl algebra An​(𝕜)A_{n}(\Bbbk). This is the classical construction relating JCn\mathrm{JC}_{n} to the Dixmier conjecture [10, 28]. The name of the derivations in [15] refers to the generalized Hamiltonian dynamics of Nambu [23]. By Cramer’s rule,

δi​(P)=(detJ​F)−1​{F1,…,Fi−1,P,Fi+1,…,Fn},{f1,…,fn}=detJ⁡(f1,…,fn),\delta_{i}(P)=(\det JF)^{-1}\{F_{1},\dots,F_{i-1},P,F_{i+1},\dots,F_{n}\},\qquad\{f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\}=\det J(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}),

where {}\{\ \} is the Nambu bracket [23, 27]. Thus δi\delta_{i} is, up to a constant factor, the Nambu–Hamiltonian vector field of the n−1n-1 functions FjF_{j}, j≠ij\neq i, and (iv) is the preservation of volume by such fields [23, 27]. If FF is only assumed to satisfy c=detJ​F≠0c=\det JF\neq 0, then (1) defines derivations of KK, and the Piola identity gives divδi=∑k∂k(c−1adj(JF)k​i)=−δi(c)/c\operatorname{div}\delta_{i}=\sum_{k}\partial_{k}\bigl(c^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(JF)_{ki}\bigr)=-\delta_{i}(c)/c. Since ∂k=∑i(JF)i​kδi\partial_{k}=\sum_{i}(JF)_{ik}\delta_{i}, all δi\delta_{i} have zero divergence if and only if c∈𝕜×c\in\Bbbk^{\times}, that is, if and only if FF is a Keller map. For a gradient F=∇hF=\nabla h the derivation δi\delta_{i} is the derivative with respect to pi=∂ihp_{i}=\partial_{i}h written in the coordinates XX.

3. The criterion of [5] and its converse

Let δi\delta_{i} act on K⊗𝕜RK\otimes_{\Bbbk}R by δi​(a⊗b)=δi​(a)⊗b+a⊗δi​(b)\delta_{i}(a\otimes b)=\delta_{i}(a)\otimes b+a\otimes\delta_{i}(b), let EE be the ring of constants of K⊗𝕜RK\otimes_{\Bbbk}R, and let

φ:K⊗𝕜E→K⊗𝕜R,φ⁡(a⊗e)=(a⊗1)​e.\varphi\colon K\otimes_{\Bbbk}E\to K\otimes_{\Bbbk}R,\qquad\varphi(a\otimes e)=(a\otimes 1)\,e.

By [5, Proposition 2.2] the map φ\varphi is injective, and by [5, Theorem 3.1] the surjectivity of φ\varphi implies that FF has a polynomial inverse. The equivalence below is stated in [5], and we include a proof of the converse direction.

Lemma 3.1.
  1. (i)

    im⁡φ\operatorname{im}\varphi is a 𝕜\Bbbk-subalgebra of K⊗RK\otimes R containing K⊗1K\otimes 1 and EE, and it is stable under δ1,…,δn\delta_{1},\dots,\delta_{n}.

  2. (ii)

    The elements uj=Fj⊗1−1⊗Fju_{j}=F_{j}\otimes 1-1\otimes F_{j} lie in EE.

  3. (iii)

    φ\varphi is surjective if and only if 1⊗Xi∈im⁡φ1\otimes X_{i}\in\operatorname{im}\varphi for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

Proof.

(i) φ\varphi is a homomorphism of 𝕜\Bbbk-algebras, φ⁡(a⊗1)=a⊗1\varphi(a\otimes 1)=a\otimes 1 and φ⁡(1⊗e)=e\varphi(1\otimes e)=e. Moreover δi​((a⊗1)​e)=(δi​a⊗1)​e\delta_{i}((a\otimes 1)e)=(\delta_{i}a\otimes 1)e because δi​e=0\delta_{i}e=0. (ii) δi​(uj)=δi​j−δi​j=0\delta_{i}(u_{j})=\delta_{ij}-\delta_{ij}=0 by Lemma 2.1(i). (iii) K⊗RK\otimes R is generated as a 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra by K⊗1K\otimes 1 and 1⊗X1,…,1⊗Xn1\otimes X_{1},\dots,1\otimes X_{n}. Apply (i). ∎

Proposition 3.2.

A Keller map FF has a polynomial inverse if and only if φ\varphi is bijective.

Proof.

One direction is [5, Theorem 3.1]. Conversely, let GG be the inverse of FF, so that Xi=Gi​(F)X_{i}=G_{i}(F). Since 1⊗Fj=Fj⊗1−uj1\otimes F_{j}=F_{j}\otimes 1-u_{j} in K⊗RK\otimes R, one has

1⊗Xi=Gi​(F1⊗1−u1,…,Fn⊗1−un)∈im⁡φ1\otimes X_{i}=G_{i}(F_{1}\otimes 1-u_{1},\dots,F_{n}\otimes 1-u_{n})\in\operatorname{im}\varphi

by Lemma 3.1(i),(ii). Lemma 3.1(iii) and [5, Proposition 2.2] conclude. ∎

4. Gradient maps and the Legendre potential

Let hh be a Keller potential, F=∇hF=\nabla h, ℋ=Hess⁡h=J​F\mathcal{H}=\operatorname{Hess}h=JF, and

(2) g:=⟨X,∇h⟩−h=∑i=1nXi​∂ih−h∈𝕜⁡[X].g:=\langle X,\nabla h\rangle-h=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\,\partial_{i}h-h\in\Bbbk[X].

We call gg the Legendre potential of hh.

Lemma 4.1.

δi​(g)=Xi\delta_{i}(g)=X_{i} for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

Proof.

∂kg=∑jℋk​j​Xj\partial_{k}g=\sum_{j}\mathcal{H}_{kj}X_{j}. Since ℋ\mathcal{H} is symmetric, δi=∑k(ℋ−1)i​k∂k\delta_{i}=\sum_{k}(\mathcal{H}^{-1})_{ik}\partial_{k}, and δi​(g)=∑j(ℋ−1​ℋ)i​j​Xj=Xi\delta_{i}(g)=\sum_{j}(\mathcal{H}^{-1}\mathcal{H})_{ij}X_{j}=X_{i}. ∎

Remark 4.2.

The computation uses no division by integers. Lemma 4.1 holds over any commutative ring in which detHess⁡h\det\operatorname{Hess}h is a unit.

Theorem 4.3 (single condition).

∇h\nabla h is a polynomial automorphism if and only if 1⊗g∈im⁡φ1\otimes g\in\operatorname{im}\varphi.

Proof.

If 1⊗g∈im⁡φ1\otimes g\in\operatorname{im}\varphi, then 1⊗Xi=δi​(1⊗g)∈im⁡φ1\otimes X_{i}=\delta_{i}(1\otimes g)\in\operatorname{im}\varphi by Lemmas 3.1(i) and 4.1, so φ\varphi is surjective. Proposition 3.2 gives both directions. ∎

4.1. The Legendre transform

Fix x0∈𝕜nx_{0}\in\Bbbk^{n} and put p0=∇h​(x0)p_{0}=\nabla h(x_{0}). Since ℋ⁡(x0)\mathcal{H}(x_{0}) is invertible, ∇h\nabla h has a unique formal inverse G∈𝕜​[[p−p0]]nG\in\Bbbk[[p-p_{0}]]^{n} with G⁡(p0)=x0G(p_{0})=x_{0}. The formal Legendre transform of hh at x0x_{0} is

h∗​(p):=⟨p,G⁡(p)⟩−h⁡(G⁡(p))∈𝕜⁡[[p−p0]].h^{*}(p):=\langle p,G(p)\rangle-h(G(p))\in\Bbbk[[p-p_{0}]].

By definition h∗∘∇h=gh^{*}\circ\nabla h=g.

Lemma 4.4 ([20]).

∇h∗=G\nabla h^{*}=G.

Proof.

∂pih∗=Gi+∑j(pj−(∂jh)​(G))​∂piGj=Gi\partial_{p_{i}}h^{*}=G_{i}+\sum_{j}\bigl(p_{j}-(\partial_{j}h)(G)\bigr)\partial_{p_{i}}G_{j}=G_{i}, because (∇h)​(G​(p))=p(\nabla h)(G(p))=p. ∎

Remark 4.5 (relation to [20]).

The Hessian conjecture was formulated by Meng through the formal Legendre transform [20], and independently, without the Legendre transform, by de Bondt and van den Essen [12], see the acknowledgement in [20]. Meng proves that HCn\mathrm{HC}_{n} for all nn is equivalent to JCn\mathrm{JC}_{n} for all nn [20, Proposition 1.4]. In a fixed dimension his argument gives HC2​n⇒JCn⇒HCn\mathrm{HC}_{2n}\Rightarrow\mathrm{JC}_{n}\Rightarrow\mathrm{HC}_{n}, and in particular it does not give JC2⇒HC4\mathrm{JC}_{2}\Rightarrow\mathrm{HC}_{4}. He also proves HCn\mathrm{HC}_{n} over ℝ\mathbb{R} when Hess⁡h\operatorname{Hess}h is definite at one point [20, Theorem 1.3], and gives a tree formula for the Taylor coefficients of h∗h^{*} at ∇h​(0)\nabla h(0) in terms of those of hh at 00 [20, Theorem 2.1]. Proposition 4.6 below expresses the Taylor coefficients of h∗h^{*} at ∇h​(x0)\nabla h(x_{0}), for every x0x_{0}, as values at x0x_{0} of the polynomials δα​(g)\delta^{\alpha}(g).

Proposition 4.6.

For every multi-index α\alpha, the identity δα​(g)=(∂αh∗)∘∇h\delta^{\alpha}(g)=(\partial^{\alpha}h^{*})\circ\nabla h holds in 𝕜⁡[[X−x0]]\Bbbk[[X-x_{0}]]. In particular, (∂αh∗)∘∇h(\partial^{\alpha}h^{*})\circ\nabla h is a polynomial.

Proof.

Induction on |α||\alpha|. The case α=0\alpha=0 is h∗∘∇h=gh^{*}\circ\nabla h=g. The inductive step is Lemma 2.1(ii) applied to P=∂αh∗P=\partial^{\alpha}h^{*}, the order of the derivations being irrelevant by Lemma 2.1(iii). ∎

Theorem 4.7 (Nambu tower of the Legendre potential).

Let d=deg⁡h≥2d=\deg h\geq 2 and N=(d−1)n−1+2N=(d-1)^{n-1}+2. The following are equivalent.

  1. (a)

    ∇h\nabla h is a polynomial automorphism.

  2. (b)

    h∗h^{*} is a polynomial for some, equivalently for every, x0∈𝕜nx_{0}\in\Bbbk^{n}.

  3. (c)

    For every multi-index β\beta in vv one has δui​δvβ​(gΦ)=(δF)β​(xi)\delta_{u_{i}}\delta_{v}^{\beta}(g_{\Phi})=(\delta^{F})^{\beta}(x_{i}) and δvβ​(gΦ)=⟨J​F𝖳​y,(δF)β​(x)⟩\delta_{v}^{\beta}(g_{\Phi})=\langle JF^{\mathsf{T}}y,(\delta^{F})^{\beta}(x)\rangle, and δα​(gΦ)=0\delta^{\alpha}(g_{\Phi})=0 whenever α\alpha contains at least two derivations δui\delta_{u_{i}}.

(i) The formal inverse of ∇Φ\nabla\Phi is (u,v)↦(GF​(v),(J​F𝖳)−1​(GF​(v))​u)(u,v)\mapsto\bigl(G_{F}(v),(JF^{\mathsf{T}})^{-1}(G_{F}(v))\,u\bigr). With x=GF​(v)x=G_{F}(v) and y=(J​F​(x)𝖳)−1​uy=(JF(x)^{\mathsf{T}})^{-1}u one gets ⟨u,x⟩+⟨v,y⟩−⟨y,F⁡(x)⟩=⟨u,x⟩\langle u,x\rangle+\langle v,y\rangle-\langle y,F(x)\rangle=\langle u,x\rangle. (ii) By Proposition 4.6, δα​(gΦ)=(∂αΦ∗)∘∇Φ\delta^{\alpha}(g_{\Phi})=(\partial^{\alpha}\Phi^{*})\circ\nabla\Phi. By (i), ∂ui∂vβΦ∗=∂vβ(GF)i\partial_{u_{i}}\partial_{v}^{\beta}\Phi^{*}=\partial_{v}^{\beta}(G_{F})_{i}, ∂vβΦ∗=⟨u,∂vβGF⟩\partial_{v}^{\beta}\Phi^{*}=\langle u,\partial_{v}^{\beta}G_{F}\rangle, and derivatives of order ≥2\geq 2 in uu vanish. Finally (∂vβGF)∘F=(δF)β​(x)(\partial_{v}^{\beta}G_{F})\circ F=(\delta^{F})^{\beta}(x) by Lemma 2.1(ii) applied to FF. ∎

Remark 5.3.

Theorem 4.7 applied to Φ\Phi, of degree deg⁡F+1\deg F+1 in 2​n2n variables, gives the order (deg⁡F)2​n−1+2(\deg F)^{2n-1}+2. Proposition 5.2(i) and [9] show that deg⁡Φ∗≤(deg⁡F)n−1+1\deg\Phi^{*}\leq(\deg F)^{n-1}+1 when FF is invertible, so the order (deg⁡F)n−1+2(\deg F)^{n-1}+2 suffices.

Theorem 5.4 (Legendre potential of the doubling).

The Legendre potential of ΦF\Phi_{F} is ⟨y,J​F​(x)​x⟩\langle y,JF(x)\,x\rangle. If F=X+HF=X+H, it equals ⟨y,x⟩+⟨y,ℰ⁡(H)⟩\langle y,x\rangle+\langle y,\mathcal{E}(H)\rangle, and if moreover HH is homogeneous of degree mm, it equals ⟨y,x⟩+m​⟨y,H⟩\langle y,x\rangle+m\langle y,H\rangle.

Proof.

By (4), ⟨x,J​F𝖳​y⟩+⟨y,F⟩−⟨y,F⟩=⟨y,J​F​x⟩\langle x,JF^{\mathsf{T}}y\rangle+\langle y,F\rangle-\langle y,F\rangle=\langle y,JF\,x\rangle. Further J⁡(X+H)​x=x+ℰ⁡(H)J(X+H)\,x=x+\mathcal{E}(H), and ℰ⁡(H)=m​H\mathcal{E}(H)=mH for HH homogeneous of degree mm. ∎

Corollary 5.5.

Let FF be a Keller map, Φ=ΦF\Phi=\Phi_{F} and N≥1N\geq 1. Then δα​(gΦ)=0\delta^{\alpha}(g_{\Phi})=0 for all |α|=N|\alpha|=N if and only if (δF)β​(xi)=0(\delta^{F})^{\beta}(x_{i})=0 for all ii and all |β|=N−1|\beta|=N-1. In particular, for the cubic homogeneous reduction of [9, 33], F=X+HF=X+H with HH cubic homogeneous, the Legendre potential of ΦF\Phi_{F} is ⟨y,x⟩+3​⟨y,H⟩\langle y,x\rangle+3\langle y,H\rangle, and Theorem 4.7 applied to ΦF\Phi_{F} is the criterion of [29, Proposition 3.1.4] applied to FF, with the order raised by one.

Proof.

By Proposition 5.2(ii), the elements δα​(gΦ)\delta^{\alpha}(g_{\Phi}) with |α|=N|\alpha|=N are 00, (δF)β​(xi)(\delta^{F})^{\beta}(x_{i}) with |β|=N−1|\beta|=N-1, and ⟨J​F𝖳​y,(δF)β​(x)⟩\langle JF^{\mathsf{T}}y,(\delta^{F})^{\beta}(x)\rangle with |β|=N|\beta|=N, according as α\alpha contains at least two, exactly one or no derivation δui\delta_{u_{i}}. The elements of the third kind vanish if those of the second kind vanish, since (δF)β=δjF​(δF)β′(\delta^{F})^{\beta}=\delta^{F}_{j}(\delta^{F})^{\beta^{\prime}} for some jj and |β′|=N−1|\beta^{\prime}|=N-1. ∎

Remark 5.6.

The symmetric lift was introduced in [12] to reduce JCn\mathrm{JC}_{n} to Keller maps with symmetric Jacobian matrix. Corollary 5.5 shows that, for the criterion of Theorem 4.7, the doubled potential gives no condition beyond the criterion for FF itself. In particular, in the setting of Nambu derivations the passage from JCn\mathrm{JC}_{n} to HC2​n\mathrm{HC}_{2n} does not simplify the verification of invertibility.

5.1. The cotangent lift of a vector field

Let VV be a polynomial vector field on 𝕜n\Bbbk^{n} and fV​(q,p)=⟨p,V⁡(q)⟩f_{V}(q,p)=\langle p,V(q)\rangle its momentum function on T∗​𝕜nT^{*}\Bbbk^{n} with the form ∑d​qi∧d​pi\sum dq_{i}\wedge dp_{i}. The Hamiltonian vector field of fVf_{V} is V^=(V⁡(q),−J​V​(q)𝖳​p)\hat{V}=(V(q),-JV(q)^{\mathsf{T}}p), the cotangent lift of [8] used in [17].

Proposition 5.7.
  1. (i)

    detHess⁡fV=(−1)n​(detJ​V)2\det\operatorname{Hess}f_{V}=(-1)^{n}(\det JV)^{2}. Thus fVf_{V} is a Keller potential if and only if VV is a Keller map.

  2. (ii)

    Over ℂ\mathbb{C}, if ϕt\phi_{t} is the local flow of VV, then the flow of V^\hat{V} is T∗​ϕt​(q,p)=(ϕt​(q),(J​ϕt​(q)𝖳)−1​p)T^{*}\phi_{t}(q,p)=\bigl(\phi_{t}(q),(J\phi_{t}(q)^{\mathsf{T}})^{-1}p\bigr).

  3. (iii)

    For F=X+HF=X+H one has ΦF=⟨y,x⟩+fH\Phi_{F}=\langle y,x\rangle+f_{H}, and the Legendre potential of ΦF\Phi_{F} is ⟨y,x⟩+fℰ⁡(H)\langle y,x\rangle+f_{\mathcal{E}(H)}.

Proof.

(i) The second derivatives of ∑iVi​(q)​pi\sum_{i}V_{i}(q)p_{i} form the blocks ∑ipi​Hess⁡Vi\sum_{i}p_{i}\operatorname{Hess}V_{i}, J​V𝖳JV^{\mathsf{T}}, J​VJV and 00. The Laplace expansion as in Proposition 5.1 gives the determinant. (ii) Hamilton’s equations for fVf_{V} are q˙=V⁡(q)\dot{q}=V(q) and p˙=−J​V​(q)𝖳​p\dot{p}=-JV(q)^{\mathsf{T}}p. Fix q0q_{0} and put At=J​ϕt​(q0)A_{t}=J\phi_{t}(q_{0}). The variational equation A˙t=J​V​(ϕt​(q0))​At\dot{A}_{t}=JV(\phi_{t}(q_{0}))A_{t}, A0=IA_{0}=I, gives

dd​t​(At𝖳)−1=−(At𝖳)−1​A˙t𝖳​(At𝖳)−1=−J​V​(ϕt​(q0))𝖳​(At𝖳)−1.\tfrac{d}{dt}(A_{t}^{\mathsf{T}})^{-1}=-(A_{t}^{\mathsf{T}})^{-1}\dot{A}_{t}^{\mathsf{T}}(A_{t}^{\mathsf{T}})^{-1}=-JV(\phi_{t}(q_{0}))^{\mathsf{T}}(A_{t}^{\mathsf{T}})^{-1}.

Hence t↦(ϕt​(q0),(At𝖳)−1​p0)t\mapsto\bigl(\phi_{t}(q_{0}),(A_{t}^{\mathsf{T}})^{-1}p_{0}\bigr) solves Hamilton’s equations with initial value (q0,p0)(q_{0},p_{0}), and uniqueness of solutions gives the claim. (iii) ⟨y,x+H⁡(x)⟩=⟨y,x⟩+fH\langle y,x+H(x)\rangle=\langle y,x\rangle+f_{H}, and Theorem 5.4. ∎

Remark 5.8.

By [8] the differential Galois groups of the variational equations of VV and of V^\hat{V} are isomorphic. Proposition 5.7(iii) identifies the nonlinear part of the doubled potential of a Keller map X+HX+H with the momentum function of HH, and its Legendre potential with the momentum function of ℰ⁡(H)\mathcal{E}(H). We do not draw a consequence for the Jacobian conjecture from this identification. The example of [17, Example 3.2] is a gradient field ∇P\nabla P with nonconstant detHess⁡P\det\operatorname{Hess}P, hence not a Keller map.

6. The Pascal–Legendre series

Throughout this section F=X+H∈𝕜​[X]nF=X+H\in\Bbbk[X]^{n} with t:=mini⁡ord⁡Hi≥2t:=\min_{i}\operatorname{ord}H_{i}\geq 2, and ΔF​(Q)=Q∘F−Q\Delta_{F}(Q)=Q\circ F-Q for Q∈𝕜⁡[[X]]Q\in\Bbbk[[X]]. Recall [2] that FF is Pascal finite if ΔFm​(X)=0\Delta_{F}^{m}(X)=0 for some mm, and that in characteristic zero this holds if and only if FF is the exponential of a locally nilpotent derivation.

Lemma 6.1 (scalar form of [6, Lemma 2, Theorem 5]).

For Q∈𝕜⁡[[X]]Q\in\Bbbk[[X]] with Q⁡(0)=0Q(0)=0 one has ord⁡ΔFk​Q≥ord⁡Q+k⁡(t−1)\operatorname{ord}\Delta_{F}^{k}Q\geq\operatorname{ord}Q+k(t-1). The series ∑k≥0(−1)k​ΔFk​Q\sum_{k\geq 0}(-1)^{k}\Delta_{F}^{k}Q converges in the (X)(X)-adic topology and equals Q∘F−1Q\circ F^{-1}, where F−1F^{-1} is the formal inverse.

For a monomial MM of degree rr the lowest term of M∘F−MM\circ F-M has degree ≥r+t−1\geq r+t-1. Hence ΔF\Delta_{F} raises the order by at least t−1≥1t-1\geq 1, the operator ∑k(−ΔF)k\sum_{k}(-\Delta_{F})^{k} converges and is inverse to σF=id+ΔF:Q↦Q∘F\sigma_{F}=\mathrm{id}+\Delta_{F}\colon Q\mapsto Q\circ F. On the other hand σF−1=σF−1\sigma_{F}^{-1}=\sigma_{F^{-1}}. ∎

Remark 6.3.

For h=12​⟨X,X⟩−Ph=\frac{1}{2}\langle X,X\rangle-P with PP homogeneous of degree 44 and Hess⁡P\operatorname{Hess}P nilpotent, Zhao [31, 32] writes the inverse of X−∇PX-\nabla P as X+∇QX+\nabla Q with Q=∑m≥0△m​(Pm+1)2m​m!​(m+1)!Q=\sum_{m\geq 0}\frac{\triangle^{m}(P^{m+1})}{2^{m}m!(m+1)!}, and the vanishing conjecture △m​(Pm+1)=0\triangle^{m}(P^{m+1})=0 for m≫0m\gg 0 is the statement that this series terminates. For such PP neither Zhao’s series nor the series of Proposition 6.2 terminates.

Remark 6.11.

Remark 6.12.

By Theorem 4.17 and Remark 4.18, for h=ϕ0h=\phi_{0} the normal form of gg modulo a Gröbner basis of (∂1ϕ0−T1,…,∂4ϕ0−T4)(\partial_{1}\phi_{0}-T_{1},\dots,\partial_{4}\phi_{0}-T_{4}) for a block order with z≫Tz\gg T is r=ψ0​(T)r=\psi_{0}(T). Let u=1+x1​x2u=1+x_{1}x_{2},

and Ψ=A2+13​A+2​B∈ℤ⁡[x1,x2,y1,y2,y3]\Psi=A^{2}+13A+2B\in\mathbb{Z}[x_{1},x_{2},y_{1},y_{2},y_{3}]. Then deg⁡Ψ=14\deg\Psi=14, detHess⁡Ψ=128\det\operatorname{Hess}\Psi=128, and ∇Ψ​(P+)=∇Ψ​(P−)=(0,0,−12,0,0)\nabla\Psi(P_{+})=\nabla\Psi(P_{-})=(0,0,-\frac{1}{2},0,0) for P±=(±1,∓32,0,0,0)P_{\pm}=(\pm 1,\mp\frac{3}{2},0,0,0) [21, Theorem 6.1]. Consequently, for h=Ψh=\Psi and every N≥1N\geq 1 there is a multi-index α\alpha with |α|=N|\alpha|=N and δα​(g)≠0\delta^{\alpha}(g)\neq 0, and for a normal form Ψ~\tilde{\Psi} of Ψ\Psi and its Legendre potential g~\tilde{g} one has Δ∇Ψ~k​(g~)≠0\Delta_{\nabla\tilde{\Psi}}^{k}(\tilde{g})\neq 0 for every kk, by Corollary 6.5. In particular, the symmetry of the Hessian, the constancy of the Hessian determinant and the identity δi​(g)=Xi\delta_{i}(g)=X_{i} do not by themselves imply that the formal Legendre transform is a polynomial.

Proof.

Since ∇Ψ\nabla\Psi is not injective, it has no inverse, and by Theorem 4.7, Ψ∗\Psi^{*} is not a polynomial. Apply Theorem 4.7 in the form valid for every order, and Corollary 6.5. ∎

Remark 7.2.

The potential Ψ\Psi has all properties of a Keller potential used in Sections 2, 3, 4 and 6. The matrix J∇Ψ=HessΨJ\nabla\Psi=\operatorname{Hess}\Psi is symmetric with constant determinant, the Nambu derivations of ∇Ψ\nabla\Psi are derivations of ℚ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{Q}[x,y], and δi​(gΨ)\delta_{i}(g_{\Psi}) is the ii-th coordinate function for the Legendre potential gΨg_{\Psi}. The criteria of the paper recognize the non-invertibility of ∇Ψ\nabla\Psi. By Theorems 4.7 and 4.17, for every N≥1N\geq 1 some δα​(gΨ)\delta^{\alpha}(g_{\Psi}) with |α|=N|\alpha|=N is nonzero, and gΨ∉𝕜⁡[∂1Ψ,…,∂5Ψ]g_{\Psi}\notin\Bbbk[\partial_{1}\Psi,\dots,\partial_{5}\Psi]. Since a Keller map which is birational is an automorphism [9, Chapter I, Theorem 2.1], one has μ⁡(∇Ψ)≥2\mu(\nabla\Psi)\geq 2, and by Theorem 4.15 the minimal polynomial of gΨg_{\Psi} over 𝕜⁡(∇Ψ)\Bbbk(\nabla\Psi) has degree μ⁡(∇Ψ)≥2\mu(\nabla\Psi)\geq 2. Moreover, since Ψ∗\Psi^{*} is not a polynomial, [20, Theorem 1.3] shows that Hess⁡Ψ\operatorname{Hess}\Psi is indefinite at every point of ℝ5\mathbb{R}^{5}. Over ℝ\mathbb{R} every counterexample to HCn\mathrm{HC}_{n} has this property.
